procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated August 30, 1967 of the Assam and Nagaland High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 115 of 1964, which enhanced the sentence of the appellants to death.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Iman Ali filed an appeal in the High Court of Assam and Nagaland. The High Court issued a notice to Iman Ali to show cause why his sentence should not be enhanced to the sentence of death. A similar notice was issued *suo motu* to Jogesh Chandra Arjya. The High Court affirmed the findings of fact of the Court of Session and enhanced the sentence of both appellants to death.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants sought leave from the High Court to appeal to the Supreme Court, but leave was refused. Thereupon, both of them sought special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution, which was granted by the Supreme Court on December 8, 1967.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in enhancing the sentence of the appellants from imprisonment for life to the sentence of death.

facts: The appellants were convicted under s. 396 of the Indian Penal Code for committing dacoity during which they shot and killed two inmates of a house.
The trial court (Court of Session) sentenced them to imprisonment for life but did not provide any reasons for choosing this sentence over the death penalty.
On appeal, the High Court issued a notice to the appellants to show cause why their sentences should not be enhanced to death.
After a hearing, the High Court enhanced the sentence for both appellants to death.
law: The Supreme Court referenced the principle from *Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab*, which states that an appellate court should only enhance a sentence from life imprisonment to death for the strongest possible reasons.

According to this principle, an appellate court can interfere with a trial judge's discretion on sentencing only if that discretion was improperly exercised, for example, if no reasons were given for awarding the lesser penalty.

The Court also distinguished between cases of constructive liability under s. 396 IPC (where all members of a dacoity gang are held guilty for a murder committed by one) and cases where there is direct evidence that a particular accused committed the murder themselves.
application: The Supreme Court found that the principle from *Dalip Singh* did not support the appellants' case because the trial court had failed to give any reasons for imposing life imprisonment instead of the death penalty. This failure to provide reasons constituted an improper exercise of discretion, justifying the High Court's intervention.

The Court rejected the argument that the standards for a s. 396 IPC conviction are different from a s. 302 IPC (murder) conviction in this instance. It noted that this was not a case of constructive liability.
There was a clear finding that the appellants themselves had committed the "cold-blooded murder" of two people who had not offered any resistance.

The Court concluded that the offence was just as heinous as a murder under s. 302, and in the absence of any justification from the trial court for the lesser sentence, the High Court was right to enhance it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal, holding that the High Court was justified in enhancing the sentence from life imprisonment to death. This was because the trial court had improperly exercised its discretion by giving no reasons for the lesser sentence, and the appellants had been found to have directly committed a heinous and cold-blooded double murder during the dacoity.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants for the offence under Section 396 of the Indian Penal Code was justified.

facts: The appellants, along with about 11 to 13 others, committed dacoity in a house.
During the dacoity, one appellant, Iman Ali, shot and killed an inmate named Golapi.
The other appellant, Jogesh Chandra Arjya, then shot and killed another inmate, Tenu Arjya.
The murders were described as 'cold-blooded' and were committed against victims who had not offered any resistance, with the sole object of facilitating the dacoity.
law: Section 396 of the Indian Penal Code pertains to the offence of dacoity with murder.
A conviction under this section can be based on 'constructive liability', where a person is held guilty for a murder committed by another member of the dacoity gang.
Alternatively, a conviction can be based on direct evidence that the accused personally committed the murder during the dacoity.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the appellants' conviction was not based on constructive liability.
Instead, there was a clear finding by both the Court of Session and the High Court that each of the appellants had personally committed a murder.

The Court emphasized that because the appellants were the direct perpetrators of the heinous, cold-blooded murders, they could not take advantage of the fact that their conviction was under Section 396 (dacoity with murder) rather than Section 302 (murder).
The Court found the offence to be no less serious than a standalone murder under Section 302.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge and upheld the conviction, finding it was justified because there was clear evidence that the appellants had personally and directly committed the two murders during the commission of the dacoity.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in enhancing the sentence of the appellants from imprisonment for life to the sentence of death.
appellant_arguments: Citing the case of Lal Singh v. Emperor, the power to enhance a sentence from life imprisonment to death should be exercised very rarely and only for the strongest possible reasons.

The discretion on sentencing belongs to the trial judge, and an appellate court can only interfere if that discretion has been improperly exercised (e.g., no reasons are given and none can be inferred).
respondent_arguments: The principle cited by the appellants is not applicable because the trial court awarded the sentence of life imprisonment without giving any reasons for not imposing the death penalty.
The appellants committed a cold-blooded murder of two inmates who offered no resistance, making the offence under Section 396 IPC as heinous as murder under Section 302 IPC.
The trial court's failure to provide reasons for the lesser sentence means it did not exercise its discretion judicially, which justifies the High Court's interference to enhance the sentence.

cases.case_name: Dalip Singh & Ors. v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: An appellate court's power to enhance a sentence (from transportation/life imprisonment to death) should be exercised very rarely and only for the strongest possible reasons. An appellate court can only interfere on the ground that the trial judge's discretion was improperly exercised.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An appellate court is justified in interfering with a trial court's sentencing discretion and enhancing a sentence when that discretion has been improperly exercised. Discretion is considered improperly exercised if the trial court gives no reasons for awarding a lesser penalty in a case where the facts are particularly gross, such as a cold-blooded murder.
obiter: The general rule that a sentence of death is not necessary for a conviction under s. 396, I.P.C. (dacoity with murder) applies to cases where all members of a gang are held constructively guilty, but not to cases where there is direct evidence that a specific accused committed the murder.
The power for an appellate court to enhance a sentence to death should be exercised very rarely and only for the strongest possible reasons.
In a case of murder, the death sentence should ordinarily be imposed unless the trying Judge, for reasons which should be recorded, considers it proper to award the lesser penalty.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was justified in enhancing the sentence from life imprisonment to death because the trial court failed to exercise its judicial discretion properly by not providing any reasons for awarding the lesser sentence. Furthermore, the appellants were not convicted on the basis of constructive liability but on direct evidence that they each committed a cold-blooded murder of unresisting victims, making the offence under Section 396 IPC as heinous as a murder under Section 302 IPC, thus warranting the death penalty.
legal_tests_applied: An appellate court can interfere with a trial judge's sentencing discretion if that discretion has been improperly exercised, such as when no reasons are given for the sentence and none can be inferred from the circumstances of the case.
why_appellant_lost: The principle that an appellate court should not interfere with a trial judge's sentencing discretion is not applicable because the trial court awarded the sentence of life imprisonment without giving any reasons at all for adopting that course.

The precedent cited by the appellants, which suggests a lesser sentence for an offence under Section 396 IPC, applies only to cases of constructive liability where the specific individual who committed the murder is unknown, not to cases like this where there is direct evidence that the appellants themselves committed the murders.

The conviction under Section 396 IPC was not based on constructive liability; there was a clear finding that each appellant committed a cold-blooded murder by shooting two inmates who had not even tried to put up any resistance.
why_respondent_won: The trial court's failure to give any reasons for not awarding the death sentence meant that its discretion was not exercised judicially, justifying the High Court's interference to enhance the sentence.
The offence committed by the appellants was as heinous as an offence under Section 302 IPC, as they committed a cold-blooded murder of two unresisting individuals simply to facilitate a dacoity.
The finding that the appellants personally committed the murders distinguishes this case from those involving constructive liability, where a lesser sentence might be considered.
